messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq is a 22-year-old Lebanese-American man working as a junior auditor at a mid-sized accounting firm in Chicago. He presented for therapy approximately eight months after being sexually assaulted by an acquaintance — a man he had met through a mutual friend and had agreed to meet for what he understood to be a casual social evening. The assault took place in a private apartment he had never visited before, and it involved a degree of physical restraint and coercion that left Tariq not only traumatised but profoundly disoriented about how the evening had unfolded. In the weeks that followed, he told no one. He returned to work, filed his spreadsheets, attended team meetings, and said nothing — because to say something, he had come to believe, would be to expose something shameful about himself rather than something criminal that had been done to him.

The sensory residue of that night proved relentless. A particular cologne — something cedar-heavy and synthetic — became the most reliable ambush. Tariq encountered it on a colleague who wore it every Thursday, and on those mornings he would find himself suddenly back in that apartment, his body rigid, his chest tight, the memory arriving not as recollection but as reinstatement. Smells of that register, the sight of someone behaving in a way he perceived as predatory or disrespectful toward others, and — perhaps most painfully — any phrase that echoed language his assailant had used, language he associated with a man who had since become a ghostly presence in certain social circles, all functioned as portals back to the assault. Each time a trigger fired, it brought with it a fresh wave of self-indictment: he was certain that someone else — someone more streetwise, more masculine, less naive — would never have ended up in that room. He had come to feel permanently marked by the humiliation of what had happened, and the grief of his former self — the version of him that used to find genuine pleasure in his friendships and his work — felt irretrievable.

These appraisals did not stay abstract. They drove behaviour. Because he believed the humiliation was visible, legible on his face or body, Tariq began wearing loose, layered clothing to the office — hoodies beneath blazers, scarves in mild weather — as though fabric could absorb what he feared others might read in him. He positioned himself near exits in every room: conference rooms, the break room, the elevator lobby. When a performance review was scheduled, he called in sick. The avoidance of evaluation had become so entrenched that his manager had noted it in passing, asking whether Tariq was struggling with the workload — a question that mortified him and deepened his sense that something ruined was now visible after all. He refused to visit client sites he had not been to before, unwilling to enter spaces whose layout and exits he could not pre-map in his mind.

Tariq's body had not returned to baseline. He felt it constantly braced — shoulders raised, jaw set, a low hum of readiness that never fully quieted. Sudden movements from colleagues passing behind his desk sent a spike of alarm through him that took minutes to subside. This chronic physiological vigilance meant that ordinary office life — people crossing his field of vision, a door swinging open — became a continuous source of threat signals, and those signals in turn made the triggers more sensitive, the threshold for re-experiencing lower. The concealing clothing and the exit-monitoring, which had begun as attempts to manage fear, had over months become their own kind of trap: the strategies kept his attention locked on threat, kept the body primed, and made the world feel no safer — only more surveilled. And in the moments when the strategies failed to prevent distress, Tariq took this as further evidence that he was uniquely damaged, uniquely unable to protect himself, uniquely responsible for what had been done to him.

What finally brought him to seek help was a panic response during a routine team lunch at a restaurant he had not visited before. He left abruptly, gave no explanation, and spent twenty minutes in his car. Sitting there, he thought: this is not living. He came to therapy hoping, cautiously, that he might one day stop feeling like a man who deserved what happened to him. What he feared most was that a therapist would confirm it.
